source_text: Εἶτα ὅτι μὲν ὑφ᾿ ὧν ὠνόμαζε μαθητῶν προὐδόθη. ἔμαθεν ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος ἀπὸ τῶν εὐαγγελίων, πολλοὺς εἰπὼν μαθητὰς τὸν ἕνα Ἰούδαν, ἵνα δόξῃ αὔξειν τὴν κατηγορίαν· οὐκέτι δὲ πάντα τὰ περὶ τοῦ Ἰούδα ἀναγεγραμμένα περιειργάσατο, ὅτι μαχομέναις καὶ ἐναντίαις κρίσεσι περιπεσὼν ὁ Ἰούδας περὶ τοῦ διδασκάλου οὔθ᾿ ὅλῃ ψυχῇ γέγονε κατ᾿ αὐτοῦ οὐδ᾿ ὅλῃ ψυχῇ ἐτήρησε τὴν αἰδὼ πρὸς διδάσκαλον φοιτητοῦ. „ὁ γὰρ παραδιδοὺς αὐτὸν ἔδωκε“ τῷ ἐληλυθότι ἐπὶ τὸ συλλαβεῖν τὸν Ἰησοῦν „σημεῖον“ ὄχλῳ ,.λέγων· ὃν ἂν φιλήσω, αὐτός ἐστι· κρατήσατε αὐτὸν,“ σῴζων τι τῆς πρὸς αὐτὸν αἰδοῦς· εἰ γὰρ μὴ ἔσῳζεν αὐτὴν, κἂν μετὰ παῤῥησίας χωρὶς προσποιήσεως φιλήματος παρέδωκεν αὐτόν. τοῦτο μὲν οὖν οὐ πάντας πείσει περὶ τῆς τοῦ Ἰούδα προαιρέσεως, ὅτι μετὰ τῆς φιλαργυρίας καὶ τῆς μοχθηρᾶς εἰς τὸ προδοῦναι τὸν διδάσκαλον προαιρέσεως εἶχέ τι ἀναμεμιγμένον ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ ἀπὸ τῶν Ἰησοῦ λόγων αὐτῷ ἐγγεγενημένον, ἔμφασιν ἔχον λείμματος. ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, χρηστότητος; γέγραπται γὰρ ὅτι „ἰδὼν Ἰούδας ὁ παραδιδοὺς αὐτὸν ὅτι κατεκρίθη, μεταμεληθεὶς ἔστρεψε τὰ τριάκοντα ἀργύρια τοῖς ἀρχιερεῦσι καὶ πρεσβυτέροις λέγων· ἥμαρτον παραδοὺς αἷμα δίκαιον. οἱ δὲ εἶπον· τί πρὸς ἡμᾶς; σὺ ὄψει. καὶ ῥίψας τὰ ἀργύρια εἰς τὸν ναὸν ἀνεχώρησε, καὶ ἀπελθὼν ἀπήγξατο.“ εἰ δ᾿ ὁ φιλάργυρος Ἰούδας καὶ κλέπτων τὰ εἰς λόγον τῶν πενήτων εἰς „τὸ γλωσσόκομον“ βαλλόμενα „μεταμεληθεὶς ἔστρεψε τὰ τριάκοντα ἀργύρια τοῖς ἀρχιερεῦσι καὶ πρεσβυτέροις,“ δῆλον ὅτι δεδύνηταί τινα μεταμέλειαν ἐμποιῆσαι αὐτῷ τὰ Ἰησοῦ μαθήματα, οὐ πανταχῇ καταφρονηθέντα ὑπὸ τοῦ προδότου καὶ ἀποπτυσθέντα· ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ „ἥμαρτον παραδοὺς αἷμα δίκαιον“ ἐξομολογουμένου ἦν τὸ ἡμαρτημένον. ὅρα δὲ ὅση διάπυρος καὶ σφοδρὰ γέγονεν αὐτῷ ἀπὸ μεταμελείας τῆς ἐπὶ τοῖς ἡμαρτημένοις λύπη, ὡς μηδὲ τὸ ζῆν αὐτὸν ἔτι ὑπομεῖναι ἀλλ᾿ „εἰς τὸν ναὸν“ ῥίψαντα τὸ ἀργύριον ἀναχωρῆσαι καὶ ἀπελθεῖν καὶ ἀπάγξασθαι. ἑαυτὸν γὰρ κατεδίκασε δεικνὺς ὅσον ἐδύνατο καὶ ἐν τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ τῷ Ἰούδᾳ τῷ κλέπτῃ καὶ προδότῃ ἡ Ἰησοῦ διδασκαλία, οὐ δυνηθέντι πάντῃ καταφρονῆσαι ὧν ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μεμάθηκεν. ἢ τὰ μὲν ἐμφαίνοντα τὸ μὴ πάντῃ ἀποστατικὸν τοῦ Ἰούδα καὶ μετὰ τὰ τετολμημένα κατὰ τοῦ διδασκάλου πλάσματα ἐροῦσιν οἱ περὶ τὸν Κέλσον, μόνον δ᾿ ἀληθὲς ὅτι εἷς τῶν μαθητῶν προέδωκεν αὐτὸν, καὶ προσθήσουσι τῷ γεγραμμένῳ ὅτι καὶ ὅλῃ ψυχῇ προέδωκεν αὐτόν; ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἀπίθανον, ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν γραμμάτων πάντα ὡς ἐχθρὸν ποιεῖν, καὶ τὸ πιστεύειν καὶ τὸ ἀπιστεῖν. εἰ δὲ δεῖ καὶ περὶ τοῦ Ἰούδα δυσωπητικόν τινα παραθέσθαι λόγον, φήσομεν ὅτι ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ τῶν ψαλμῶν ὅλος ὁ ἑκατοστὸς ὄγδοος ψαλμὸς τὴν περὶ τοῦ Ἰούδα περιέχει προφητείαν, οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· „ὁ θεὸς, τὴν αἴνεσίν μου μὴ παρασιωπήσῃς, ὅτι στόμα ἁμαρτωλοῦ καὶ στόμα δολίου ἐπ᾿ ἐμὲ ἠνοίχθη.“ προφητεύεται δ᾿ ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ ὅτι Ἰούδας τοῦ μὲν τῶν ἀποστόλων ἀπεχώρισεν ἑαυτὸν διὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἀριθμοῦ, εἰς δὲ τὸν τόπον αὐτοῦ ἕτερος ἐνεκρίθη· καὶ τοῦτο δηλοῦται ἐν τῷ „καὶ τὴν ἐπισκοπὴν αὐτοῦ λάβοι ἕτερος.“ ἀλλὰ γὰρ φέρε ὑπό τινος τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτὸν προδεδόσθαι χεῖρον ἢ Ἰούδας διατεθέντος καὶ ὡσπερεὶ ἐκχέαντος πάντας οὓς ἤκουσε παρὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ λόγους· τί τοῦτο πρὸς κατηγορίαν Ἰησοῦ ἢ χριστιανισμοῦ συμβάλλεται; καὶ πῶς τοῦτο ψευδῆ τὸν λόγον ἀποδείκνυσιν; ἀπελογησάμεθα δὲ περὶ τῶν ἑξῆς καὶ ἐν τοῖς πρὸ τούτων, δεικνύντες ὅτι οὐ φεύγων ἑάλω ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἀλλ᾿ ἑκὼν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν πάντων παρέδωκεν ἑαυτόν. ᾧ ἀκόλουθόν ἐστιν ὅτι, εἰ καὶ ἐδέθη, ἑκὼν ἐδέθη, διδάσκων μὴ ἀκουσίως ἡμᾶς ὑπὲρ εὐσεβείας ταῦτα ἀναλαμβάνειν.
pass_a_gloss: Then, that he was betrayed (προδίδωμι) by those whom he named (ὀνομάζω) disciples (μαθητής), the Jew in Celsus learned from the Gospels, saying 'many disciples' of the one Judas, so that he might seem to increase (αὐξάνω) the accusation (κατηγορία); but no longer did he busy himself about (περιεργάζομαι) all the things recorded about Judas, that Judas, having fallen into warring (μάχομαι) and opposite (ἐναντίος) judgements (κρίσις) about the teacher (διδάσκαλος), neither with whole soul (ψυχή) was against him nor with whole soul kept (τηρέω) the reverence/respect (αἰδώς) of a pupil (φοιτητής) toward a teacher. For 'he who betrays him gave' to the crowd (ὄχλος) that had come to seize (συλλαμβάνω) Jesus 'a sign (σημεῖον), saying: whomever I kiss (φιλέω), he it is; hold (κρατέω) him', preserving (σῴζω) something of his reverence toward him; for if he did not preserve it, he would have betrayed him with openness (παρρησία) without pretence (προσποίησις) of a kiss (φίλημα). This then will it not persuade all about the choice/purpose (προαίρεσις) of Judas, that with love of money (φιλαργυρία) and the wicked (μοχθηρός) purpose toward betraying the teacher he had something mixed (ἀναμίγνυμι) in the soul, engendered (ἐγγίνομαι) in him from Jesus’ words, having an appearance (ἔμφασις) of a remnant (λεῖμμα), so to name it, of goodness/kindness (χρηστότης)? For it is written that 'Judas who betrays him, seeing that he was condemned (κατακρίνω), having repented (μεταμέλομαι) returned (στρέφω) the thirty silver pieces (ἀργύριον) to the chief priests and elders saying: I sinned (ἁμαρτάνω) betraying righteous/innocent (δίκαιος) blood. They said: what to us? you will see. And throwing the silver into the temple he withdrew (ἀναχωρέω), and going away hanged himself (ἀπάγχομαι).' If the money-loving Judas, also stealing (κλέπτω) what was thrown into 'the money box (γλωσσόκομον)' on account of the poor (πένης), 'repented and returned the thirty silver pieces to chief priests and elders', clearly Jesus’ teachings (μάθημα) were able to produce (ἐμποιέω) some repentance (μεταμέλεια) in him, not in every way despised (καταφρονέω) by the traitor (προδότης) and spat out (ἀποπτύω); but also 'I sinned betraying innocent blood' was of one confessing (ἐξομολογέομαι) the sin. See how fiery (διάπυρος) and vehement (σφοδρός) a grief (λύπη) came to him from repentance at the sins, so that he did not even endure to live any longer, but having thrown the silver 'into the temple' withdrew and went away and hanged himself. For he condemned (καταδικάζω) himself, showing how much Jesus’ teaching (διδασκαλία) was able even in the sinner (ἁμαρτωλός) Judas, the thief (κλέπτης) and traitor, who was unable wholly to despise what he had learned from Jesus. Or will Celsus’s people say that the things showing the not wholly apostate (ἀποστατικός) state of Judas even after the deeds dared (τολμάω) against the teacher are fictions (πλάσμα), and only true that one of the disciples betrayed him, and will they add to the written that he also betrayed him with whole soul? Which is unpersuasive (ἀπίθανος): from the same writings (γράμματα) to do everything as an enemy (ἐχθρός), both believing (πιστεύω) and disbelieving (ἀπιστέω). If one must also set forth some shaming (δυσωπητικός) word about Judas, we will say that in the book of Psalms the whole hundred-and-eighth psalm contains the prophecy (προφητεία) about Judas, whose beginning: 'O God, do not pass over in silence (παρασιωπάω) my praise (αἴνεσις), for mouth of a sinner and mouth of a deceitful one (δόλιος) was opened against me.' It is prophesied in it also that Judas separated (ἀποχωρίζω) himself from the number (ἀριθμός) of the apostles because of sin, and into his place another was chosen (ἐγκρίνω); and this is shown in 'and his office of oversight (ἐπισκοπή) let another take'. But come, suppose he had been betrayed by one of the disciples disposed (διατίθημι) worse than Judas and as if pouring out (ἐκχέω) all the words he heard from Jesus; what does this contribute (συμβάλλομαι) toward accusation of Jesus or of Christianity (χριστιανισμός)? And how does this show the word/teaching (λόγος) false? We have made defence (ἀπολογέομαι) about the following points also in those before these, showing that Jesus was not caught fleeing (φεύγω) but willingly (ἑκών) on behalf of us all handed over (παραδίδωμι) himself. To which it follows that, if he was even bound (δέω), he was bound willingly, teaching us not involuntarily (ἀκουσίως) to take up (ἀναλαμβάνω) these things for piety (εὐσέβεια).
pass_b_english: Next, that he was “betrayed by those he called his disciples,” the Jew in Celsus learned from the Gospels, though he turned the one man Judas into many disciples, so as to seem to make the charge greater. But he did not go on to examine all that is recorded about Judas: that Judas fell into conflicting and opposed judgements about his teacher, and was neither against him with his whole soul, nor kept with his whole soul a pupil’s reverence for his teacher. For “he who betrayed him gave a sign” to the crowd that had come to seize Jesus, “saying, ‘The one I kiss is the man; seize him’” (Matthew 26:48). In this he kept something of his reverence for him; for had he not kept it, he would have betrayed him openly, without the pretence of a kiss.

Will this not, then, persuade everyone concerning Judas’s purpose, that together with his love of money and his wicked purpose to betray his teacher, he had something mixed into his soul, planted in him by the words of Jesus, which bore the look of a remnant, so to speak, of goodness? For it is written: “When Judas, who betrayed him, saw that he was condemned, he repented and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying, ‘I have sinned in betraying righteous blood.’ But they said, ‘What is that to us? See to it yourself.’ And throwing the pieces of silver into the temple, he withdrew, and went away and hanged himself” (Matthew 27:3–5).

If Judas, the lover of money, who also stole what was put into “the money box” for the poor (John 12:6), “repented and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders,” it is clear that the teachings of Jesus were able to produce some repentance in him, and had not been utterly despised and spat out by the traitor. Moreover, the words “I have sinned in betraying righteous blood” were those of a man confessing his sin. See how burning and violent a grief arose in him from repentance for his sins, so that he could no longer bear even to live, but threw the money “into the temple,” withdrew, went away and hanged himself. For he passed sentence on himself, and so showed how much the teaching of Jesus could do even in Judas, the sinner, the thief and the traitor, who could not utterly despise what he had learned from Jesus.

Or will Celsus and those like him say that the passages which show that Judas’s defection was not complete, even after all he dared against his teacher, are fictions, and that only this is true, that one of the disciples betrayed him? And will they add to what is written that he betrayed him with his whole soul as well? That is implausible: to act in everything as an enemy would, both believing and disbelieving the same writings.

If we must also set out an argument about Judas that will put them to shame, we shall say that in the Book of Psalms the whole of the hundred and eighth Psalm (Psalm 109) contains the prophecy about Judas. It begins: “O God, do not pass over my praise in silence, for the mouth of a sinner and the mouth of a deceiver have been opened against me” (Psalm 109:1–2). It is also prophesied in it that Judas cut himself off from the number of the apostles because of his sin, and that another was chosen in his place (Acts 1:25–26); and this is shown in the words, “And let another take his office” (Psalm 109:8).

But come, suppose he was betrayed by one of his disciples who was worse disposed than Judas, and who had, as it were, poured away every word he had heard from Jesus: what does this contribute to an accusation against Jesus or against Christianity? And how does this prove the teaching false? We have also answered the points that come next in what we said before, showing that Jesus was not caught while running away, but willingly gave himself up for us all. It follows that, even if he was bound, he was bound willingly, teaching us to take such things upon ourselves for the sake of godliness, not unwillingly.

choices.why: μέν ... δέ structure restored: the Jew learned it from the Gospels 'though he turned the one man Judas into many disciples'; 'But' moved to οὐκέτι δέ
'Will not this, then' (stiff order) changed to 'Will this not, then'; question kept as the copy-text punctuates it
Matthew 27:4 αἷμα δίκαιον: 'innocent blood' changed to 'righteous blood' in both places, since Origen's text reads δίκαιον, not ἀθῷον; note added

choices.term: ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν γραμμάτων πάντα ὡς ἐχθρὸν ποιεῖν
choices.why: ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν γραμμάτων πάντα ὡς ἐχθρὸν ποιεῖν: awkward 'treat the same writings in everything as an enemy would' made plain: 'act in everything as an enemy would, both believing and disbelieving the same writings'

checked: Matthew 26:48, Matthew 27:3-5, John 12:6, LXX Psalm 108:1-2 and 108:8 = English Psalm 109:1-2 and 109:8 (Origen's 'hundred and eighth' kept in text), Acts 1:25-26 allusion to Matthias; Celsus's Jew's phrase 'betrayed by those he called his disciples' matches 2.9 and stays in quotation marks

Scripture citations sit inline beside the clause in Pass B.

2.11 τοῦτο μὲν οὖν οὐ πάντας πείσει ... χρηστότητος; follows the copy-text and is read as a question ('Will this not, then, persuade everyone...?'). It could also be a concession ('This will not persuade everyone...'). The translator note records this; not a blocker.

translator_notes: LXX renumbering: Origen’s ‘hundred and eighth Psalm’ (ὁ ἑκατοστὸς ὄγδοος ψαλμός) is Psalm 109 in English Bibles; his number is kept in the text and the English number given in the citation. Quoted verses LXX Psalm 108:1–2 and 108:8 = English Psalm 109:1–2 and 109:8; the last is also quoted of Judas in Acts 1:20, and ‘another was chosen in his place’ alludes to the choice of Matthias (Acts 1:25–26). ‘Betrayed by those he called his disciples’ quotes Celsus’s Jew from 2.9 (ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν ... ὧν ὠνόμαζε μαθητῶν προὐδόθη). The sentence τοῦτο μὲν οὖν οὐ πάντας πείσει ... χρηστότητος; is punctuated as a question in the copy-text and translated as one; it could also be read as a concession (‘This, then, will not persuade everyone ...’), but the following γέγραπται γάρ supports the question. Matthew 27:5 ‘withdrew’ (ἀνεχώρησε) is kept. John 12:6 (γλωσσόκομον, Judas a thief) is a clear allusion; ‘for the poor’ (εἰς λόγον τῶν πενήτων) draws on John 12:5–6. ‘Willingly gave himself up for us all’ (ἑκὼν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν πάντων παρέδωκεν ἑαυτόν) is close to Romans 8:32 (ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν πάντων παρέδωκεν αὐτόν, said of the Father) and Ephesians 5:2 / Galatians 2:20 (παρέδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν); possible allusion only, not cited inline. ἐκχέαντος ... λόγους is taken as ‘poured away’ (kept nothing of) Jesus’ words. ‘Celsus and those like him’ renders οἱ περὶ τὸν Κέλσον. Matthew 27:4: Origen reads αἷμα δίκαιον (‘righteous blood’) where the common text has ἀθῷον (‘innocent’); rendered as Origen wrote it.
